title: How DNA Survives and Is Read
description: Decay chemistry, the best bones, sequencing libraries and how to prove a sequence is ancient

concepts.title: A Molecule Built to Fall Apart
concepts.contentHtml:
When an organism dies, its cells stop repairing their DNA and the molecule starts to fall apart. Two kinds of damage matter most. Water attacks the bonds that hold the purine bases, A and G, to the sugar backbone; once a base drops out, a process called depurination, the strand breaks at that point. Over thousands of years a genome of billions of letters is cut into short pieces. In Neanderthal bones the surviving fragments average less than 200 base pairs.1 The second kind of damage alters letters instead of cutting them: deamination turns cytosine (C) into uracil, which sequencing chemistry reads as thymine (T).

Can decay be measured like radioactivity? In 2012 Morten Allentoft and colleagues measured mitochondrial DNA in 158 radiocarbon-dated bones of the extinct New Zealand moa,2 all from a geographically constrained set of sites. Copy numbers fell exponentially with age, so DNA really does have a half-life. For a 242-base-pair stretch of mtDNA they estimated 521 years, which corresponds to a fragmentation rate of 5.50 × 10⁻⁶ per nucleotide per year. The formula below links the two numbers. A fragment of length \(L\) survives intact only if none of its bonds breaks, so its half-life shrinks as \(L\) grows: put in \(k = 5.5 \times 10^{-6}\) and \(L = 242\) and you get about 521 years. Short targets survive far longer than long ones.

Temperature dominates. The moa bones lay at an effective burial temperature of 13.1 °C, yet their DNA decayed almost 400 times more slowly than laboratory measurements of depurination predicted.3 Cold slows the chemistry further, so the record holders come from frozen ground. Until 2021 the oldest genomic data came from a horse 560,000 to 780,000 years old. That year van der Valk and colleagues recovered genome-wide data from three mammoth molars from northeastern Siberia, two of them more than a million years old.4 In 2022 Kjær and colleagues went further, reading environmental DNA from sediments in North Greenland dated to around two million years ago, which probably survived because it was bound to mineral surfaces.5

concepts.title: Choosing the Bone, Building the Library
concepts.contentHtml:
Where you drill matters as much as how you sequence. Most of the DNA in an archaeological bone comes from microbes that colonised it after death, and the share that belongs to the dead person, the endogenous fraction, is often tiny. In 2015 Ron Pinhasi and colleagues compared three parts of the petrous bone, the dense part of the temporal bone that encloses the inner ear. The densest region, inside the otic capsule, gave endogenous DNA fractions up to 65 times higher than the dense bone around it and up to 177 times higher than the nearby spongy bone.1 Where a skull survives, the inner ear is the obvious place to aim.

The bone powder is dissolved, and the DNA is purified and turned into a library: each fragment gets short synthetic adaptors on its ends so that a sequencer can read it. Second-generation sequencing, which reads millions of short molecules in parallel, suits ancient DNA because ancient molecules are already short, and it made shotgun sequencing of entire genomes from fossils possible. In 2012 Matthias Meyer's group in Leipzig added a single-stranded library method. Libraries are normally built from double-stranded DNA; starting from single strands doubles the representation of ancient DNA in the library,2 and it let the team build a 30-fold Denisovan genome from a scrap of finger bone.

Then comes a choice. Shotgun sequencing reads whatever is in the library, wasting most reads on microbes when the endogenous fraction is low. Capture, or hybridisation enrichment, fishes out only the fragments that overlap chosen positions in the genome. In 2015 Wolfgang Haak and colleagues enriched libraries for 394,577 variable sites, which cut the sequencing needed by a median of around 250-fold;3 a later panel known as the 1240k array targets about 1.2 million. Capture made population studies affordable. Published genome-wide data from ancient humans went from none in 2009 to more than five thousand individuals by 2021.4 The price is a filter: you see only the sites you chose to look at.

concepts.title: Proving a Sequence Is Ancient
concepts.contentHtml:
The great enemy of ancient DNA research is not decay but contamination. Everyone who handles a bone, from excavator to curator, leaves DNA on it, and modern DNA is long, undamaged and plentiful, so a few stray molecules can swamp the dead person's trace. Pääbo and others showed that Late Pleistocene bones are heavily contaminated by microbes and by the people who handled them, while the bone's own DNA, if present at all, survives only in trace amounts. Even the Neanderthal genome project stumbled: a pilot data set of close to a million base pairs, processed partly in conventional laboratories, later turned out to be 11 to 40 per cent modern human DNA.1 The remedy, which the Nobel committee credited to Pääbo, was specialised clean rooms and a demand that other laboratories reproduce results independently.2

Damage itself became the best proof of age. In 2007 Adrian Briggs and colleagues showed that in Neanderthal DNA the substitutions caused by damaged cytosines are vastly overrepresented and drastically clustered at the ends of molecules,3 where single strands leave the bases exposed. Genuine ancient reads therefore show elevated C-to-T and G-to-A changes near their ends, while other substitutions stay rare. A library of short fragments with this signature looks ancient; a library of long, pristine molecules looks modern. When Kirsten Bos and colleagues studied Black Death victims, their plague DNA showed exactly this damage pattern.

Laboratories also estimate how much contamination remains, using quirks of inheritance:

  • Mitochondrial DNA: find positions where the ancient mtDNA differs from at least 99 per cent of living humans, then count reads that carry the modern letter instead.
  • The Y chromosome: if the bones come from females, every Y-chromosome fragment must come from a contaminating male. For the 2010 Neanderthal genome, built from three female bones, this put modern male contamination at about 0.6 per cent.4
  • The nuclear genome: statistical models estimate what share of reads carry the modern rather than the ancient state across many sites.

title: Pääbo and the Neanderthal Genome
description: From a mummy to the Feldhofer bone, the 2010 draft, the D statistic and a Nobel Prize

concepts.title: From a Mummy to the Neander Valley
concepts.contentHtml:
Svante Pääbo's road to the Neanderthals began with Egypt. While studying medicine at Uppsala University he nurtured a strong interest in Egyptology, and during graduate work on adenoviruses in Per A. Peterson's group he secretly ran a side project to extract DNA from mummies. He cloned DNA from a 2,400-year-old mummy sample and found human sequences among the clones.1 He later acknowledged that the result was probably contaminated by DNA from living people, and he turned to the remains of animals, where contamination is easier to spot, to improve the methods.

The polymerase chain reaction (PCR), which copies a chosen stretch of DNA over and over, revolutionised the field in the mid-1980s. In 1988 Pääbo and Allan Wilson, in whose Berkeley laboratory he was then working, were the first to apply PCR to ancient remains.2 PCR could amplify the few molecules that survive in old bone, but it amplified a single stray modern molecule just as happily, so the risk of contamination grew rather than shrank.

The breakthrough came in 1997, from the Neanderthal type specimen itself: bones found in 1856 in the Feldhofer cave in the Neander valley near Düsseldorf. Matthias Krings, Pääbo and colleagues amplified short overlapping pieces of the mitochondrial control region, sequenced 123 clones covering 13 fragments at least twice each, and assembled 379 letters of Neanderthal mtDNA.3 The sequence fell outside the variation of modern humans, and the common ancestor of Neanderthal and modern human mtDNA came out about four times older than the common ancestor of all modern human mtDNAs.

Krings and colleagues concluded that Neanderthals went extinct without contributing mtDNA to modern humans.4 For mitochondria that was right, but mitochondria pass only from mother to child, so they reveal only whether women moved between groups. To test whether the populations had interbred at all, Pääbo needed the nuclear genome, with its tens of thousands of recombining, independently evolving segments.

concepts.title: The 2010 Draft and the D Statistic
concepts.contentHtml:
Pääbo, now at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig, which he had established, turned to the nuclear genome as new sequencing machines appeared. The material came from Vindija Cave in Croatia. One bone stood out because more than 90 per cent of its mtDNA segments were Neanderthal, and in the end three specimens, each about 40,000 years old and each containing more than 1 per cent Neanderthal DNA, were chosen for sequencing.1 Almost everything else in them was microbial. In 2010 Richard Green and a large consortium published the draft: more than 4 billion nucleotides from three individuals,2 assembled from fragments averaging under 200 base pairs.

How do you detect interbreeding? Neanderthals and modern humans share ancestors within the last 500,000 years, so even without any mixing a Neanderthal will, at some sites, match one living person better than another by chance. The test therefore looks at the balance across the whole genome. Take two living people, H1 and H2, and look at sites where the Neanderthal carries a derived allele, one that differs from the chimpanzee. Count the sites where the Neanderthal matches H1 but not H2, \(n_1\), and those where it matches H2 but not H1, \(n_2\). If neither population received Neanderthal genes, the derived alleles should match the two humans equally often, and the statistic D below should not differ significantly from zero.

The result was clear. Neanderthals shared more genetic variants with present-day people in Eurasia than with present-day people in sub-Saharan Africa.3 The simplest explanation was gene flow from Neanderthals into the ancestors of non-Africans, before the Eurasian groups diverged from one another. The draft suggested that between 1 and 4 per cent of the genomes of people in Eurasia derive from Neanderthals.4 Statistics of this kind, in many variants, became the workhorse of ancient population genetics; the Kennewick study in Lesson 7 used them too.

concepts.title: A High-Quality Genome and a Nobel Prize
concepts.contentHtml:
The 2010 draft was thin: a total of 1.3-fold coverage from three Croatian Neanderthals, so the average position was read only about once. In 2014 Kay Prüfer and colleagues published a high-quality genome from a Neanderthal woman, sequenced from a toe bone found in 2010 in Denisova Cave in the Altai Mountains. It revealed something intimate. Her parents were related at the level of half-siblings, and mating among close relatives was common among her recent ancestors.1 The analysis also detected several gene-flow events among Neanderthals, Denisovans and early modern humans, possibly including gene flow into Denisovans from an unknown archaic group.2 And it gave a definitive list of the changes that became fixed in modern humans after our ancestors separated from those of Neanderthals and Denisovans: a catalogue of what, genetically, sets us apart.

On 3 October 2022 the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet awarded Pääbo the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his discoveries concerning the genomes of extinct hominins and human evolution.3 The press release stressed three achievements: sequencing the Neanderthal genome, which it called something seemingly impossible; discovering a previously unknown hominin, Denisova; and showing that genes flowed from these extinct groups into Homo sapiens. It credited him with founding a new discipline,4 palaeogenomics.

Why a medicine prize for what is mostly history? The committee's answer was physiology: this ancient gene flow still matters today, for example in how our immune systems react to infections, a theme Lesson 4 follows. It was also a prize for method. The draft genome relied on clean rooms, on tagged sequencing adaptors attached inside the clean room to minimise contamination, and on three separate estimates of contamination from mitochondrial, Y-chromosome and nuclear DNA. Those habits are what the field inherited, and every later lesson in this topic depends on them.

title: Denisovans from a Finger Bone
description: A people known first from DNA: the Altai genomes, proteins in fossils and many Denisovan groups

concepts.title: A Genome Without a Body
concepts.contentHtml:
In 2008 excavators in Denisova Cave, in the Altai Mountains of southern Siberia, recovered the tip of a little finger: the distal phalanx of the fifth digit of a juvenile. Nothing about its shape stood out. Pääbo's group powdered it and found its DNA exceptionally well preserved. The mitochondrial genome, published by Johannes Krause and colleagues in March 2010 from 30 milligrams of bone powder, was a shock. Neanderthal mtDNA differs from that of living humans at an average of 202 positions; this one differed at an average of 385, against 1,462 for a chimpanzee.1 Its common ancestor with human and Neanderthal mtDNA lay about a million years back,2 twice as deep as the common ancestor of human and Neanderthal mitochondria.

The nuclear genome, published by David Reich, Richard Green and colleagues later that year at 1.9-fold coverage, told a different story. The finger's owner belonged to a sister group of the Neanderthals, sharing a more recent common ancestor with them than with us. The mitochondrial tree had misled, a standing reminder that one inherited unit is not a population history. The group was named after the cave. Denisovans were identified entirely from genome data, before anyone knew what they looked like.

Reich's team also found the Denisovans' living legacy. The Denisovans were not involved in the gene flow from Neanderthals into Eurasians, but they contributed 4 to 6 per cent of the genetic material of present-day Melanesians,3 thousands of kilometres to the south-east. In 2012 Matthias Meyer's single-stranded library method turned the same finger into a 30-fold genome, good enough to measure the individual's heterozygosity directly. Genetic diversity turned out to be extremely low.4 Denisovans had a small population size over the last few hundred thousand years compared with modern humans, and that small size shows in a greater accumulation of protein-changing mutations.

concepts.title: Putting Bones to the Genome
concepts.contentHtml:
For a decade Denisovans were a genome in search of a skeleton. A tooth from Denisova Cave carried a mitochondrial genome very similar to the finger's and shared no derived features with Neanderthals or modern humans, but nobody knew what a Denisovan face looked like. Most bone fragments from a cave cannot be identified by eye. In 2018 Viviane Slon and colleagues reported Denisova 11, a fragment picked out from over 2,000 undiagnostic bones using1 collagen peptide mass fingerprinting, a protein screen that sorts bone by animal group. Its genome showed a female at least 13 years old whose mother was a Neanderthal and whose father was a Denisovan.2 Finding a first-generation hybrid among so few sequenced archaic individuals suggests that mixing was common when the groups met.

Proteins can outlast DNA, and their amino acid sequences carry genetic information. In 2019 researchers used ancient protein analysis to identify a mandible from Baishiya Karst Cave near Xiahe, on the Tibetan Plateau, as Denisovan, and U-series dating of carbonate stuck to it showed that it was at least 160,000 years old.3 Archaic humans had lived at high altitude long before Homo sapiens arrived. In 2025 Tsutaya and colleagues recovered 4,241 amino acid residues from a jaw from Taiwan, Penghu 1, including two Denisovan-specific variants,4 and identified it as a male Denisovan. Its age is uncertain: either 10,000 to 70,000 or 130,000 to 190,000 years.

Also in 2025, Qiaomei Fu and colleagues turned to the nearly complete Harbin cranium from northeastern China, more than 146,000 years old.5 No DNA could be retrieved from a tooth or the petrous bone, but mitochondrial DNA survived in the dental calculus, the mineralised plaque on the teeth. It fell within Denisovan variation. For the first time a Denisovan identification was attached to a skull, so anatomists can compare Denisovans with other Middle Pleistocene fossils from East Asia.

concepts.title: Many Denisovan Peoples
concepts.contentHtml:
Denisovan ancestry in living people is not one uniform inheritance. In 2018 Sharon Browning and colleagues scanned modern genomes for archaic segments and compared each one with the Altai Denisovan genome. They found Denisovan ancestry in populations from East and South Asia and in Papuans, and it came in two components with differing similarity to the sequenced Altai Denisovan.1 That pointed to at least two distinct episodes of Denisovan admixture, from Denisovan populations with different degrees of relatedness to the finger bone's owner.

The Denisovans had a complicated past of their own. The 2014 Altai Neanderthal study had already hinted at gene flow into Denisovans from an unknown archaic group. In 2025 Stéphane Peyrégne and colleagues posted a preprint (a paper released before peer review) describing a second high-quality Denisovan genome, from a molar of a man who lived about 200,000 years ago. His small group had mixed with early Neanderthals and was then replaced by Denisovans who had mixed with later Neanderthals.2 The genomes also showed that Denisovans received genes from hominins that diverged before the ancestors of Denisovans and modern humans split.

With two good genomes, the team could divide the Denisovan ancestry of living people into contributions from at least three distinct Denisovan groups. Oceanians and South Asians independently inherited DNA from a deeply diverged Denisovan population that was probably isolated in South Asia.3 East Asians lack this component, which suggests that their ancestors arrived separately, perhaps by a northerly route. If these results hold up, the Denisovans were not one tribe in a Siberian cave but a set of populations spread across Asia, from the Altai to the Tibetan Plateau and Taiwan, still known from only a handful of bones.

title: Archaic DNA in Living People
description: Finding Neanderthal segments, dating the encounter, and the deserts and gifts it left

concepts.title: Finding the Neanderthal in a Living Genome
concepts.contentHtml:
A D statistic tells you that a population carries archaic ancestry; it does not tell you where. For that, geneticists hunt for introgressed segments: stretches of a living person's DNA that closely match an archaic genome. The difficulty is telling ancient hybridisation apart from ancestry shared since before Neanderthals and modern humans split, since both make sequences look alike. Introgressed segments give themselves away by length. They entered our lineage tens of thousands of years ago and become progressively shorter with each generation as recombination cuts them,1 but they remain far longer than the scraps of similarity left by much older shared ancestry.

Most early methods also needed a reference panel of people assumed to carry no Neanderthal ancestry, usually Africans. That assumption hid something. In 2020 Lu Chen, Joshua Akey and colleagues introduced IBDmix, a method based on identity by descent that compares each person directly with an archaic genome and needs no modern reference panel. Applied to 2,504 people from around the world, it found on average 17 million base pairs of Neanderthal sequence per individual in the African samples.2 The team explained this by migrations back into Africa, predominantly from ancestral Europeans, and by gene flow into Neanderthals from an early group of modern humans that had dispersed out of Africa.3

Other patterns are familiar but still debated. Every study of archaic admixture finds that East Asians carry roughly 20 per cent more Neanderthal ancestry than Europeans.4 One proposal is an extra pulse of mixing after the ancestors of East Asians and Europeans split; Browning's group argued that if so, the second source must have been closely related to the main admixing Neanderthals. Denisovan ancestry is patchier still: present at low levels in East and South Asians, and far higher in Papuans.

concepts.title: Dating the Encounter
concepts.contentHtml:
Recombination gives archaic segments a clock. Each generation, chromosomes exchange pieces, so a block inherited from a Neanderthal ancestor is cut a little shorter. The longer a person's Neanderthal segments, the less time has passed between the mixing and that person's life. Ancient modern humans are therefore precious: someone who lived 45,000 years ago lived much closer to the encounter than you do, carries longer Neanderthal blocks and pins down the date far more precisely.

Two recent studies used this logic. Sümer and colleagues analysed one high-coverage and five low-coverage genomes from about 45,000-year-old remains in the Ilsenhöhle at Ranis, Germany, and a further high-coverage genome from Zlatý kůň in Czechia. The individuals were distantly related and belonged to the same small, isolated population, the deepest known split from the out-of-Africa lineage. Their Neanderthal segments came from a single admixture event shared with all non-Africans, which the team dated to approximately 45,000 to 49,000 years ago.1

Iasi, Moorjani and colleagues took a wider view. They built a catalogue of Neanderthal ancestry segments in more than 300 genomes spanning the past 50,000 years and concluded that the vast majority of Neanderthal gene flow came from a single, shared, extended period between 50,500 and 43,500 years ago.2 Their best model put its duration at around 7,000 years: not one meeting but a long era of contact. Most natural selection on Neanderthal variants, both positive and negative, happened rapidly after the gene flow.

There is a striking corollary. If the ancestors of all non-Africans sequenced so far lived in one common population around 45,000 to 49,000 years ago, then modern human remains older than 50,000 years from outside Africa probably represent different non-African populations,3 branches that are not the main source of people living outside Africa today.

concepts.title: Deserts and Gifts
concepts.contentHtml:
Neanderthal ancestry is not scattered evenly. In 2014 Sriram Sankararaman, Reich and colleagues mapped it across present-day genomes and found large deserts, long regions with almost none. Part of the explanation is probably small population sizes shortly after interbreeding, but selection contributed too. Neanderthal ancestry is significantly reduced in genes specifically expressed in the testes, and there is about a 5-fold reduction on chromosome X, which is known to harbour a disproportionate share of male hybrid sterility genes.1 One reading is that some hybrids were less fertile, and selection purged the variants responsible.

Other variants were kept. Regions with a high frequency of Neanderthal alleles are enriched for genes affecting keratin filaments, part of skin and hair, which suggests that Neanderthal alleles may have helped modern humans adapt to environments outside Africa.2 The same team found Neanderthal-derived alleles associated today with lupus, biliary cirrhosis, Crohn's disease, smoking behaviour and type 2 diabetes. A variant that helped long ago need not help now.

The clearest cases of adaptive introgression are dramatic. On the Tibetan plateau, above 4,000 metres, oxygen pressure is about 40 per cent lower than at sea level. EPAS1, a hypoxia gene with the most extreme signature of positive selection in Tibetans, has a haplotype structure that Emilia Huerta-Sánchez and colleagues showed in 2014 can only be convincingly explained by introgression from Denisovans or their relatives;3 the selected haplotype is found only in Denisovans and Tibetans, and at very low frequency among Han Chinese. The pandemic supplied a sharper case. In 2020 Zeberg and Pääbo showed that the major genetic risk factor for severe COVID-19 is a segment of around 50,000 base pairs on chromosome 3 inherited from Neanderthals, carried by around 50 per cent of people in South Asia and around 16 per cent in Europe.4

title: The Yamnaya and the Remaking of Europe
description: Three ancestral streams, the 2015 steppe migration, Beaker Britain and the Indo-European question

concepts.title: Three Streams of Ancestry
concepts.contentHtml:
Living Europeans descend mainly from three ancient sources, and ancient DNA can watch each one arrive. First came the hunter-gatherers. In 2015 Wolfgang Haak, David Reich and colleagues found them arranged along a cline: western hunter-gatherers from Luxembourg, Spain and Hungary at one end, eastern hunter-gatherers from Karelia and the Samara steppe at the other, and hunter-gatherers from Sweden in between. The eastern group had a strong affinity to MA1, a 24,000-year-old individual from Siberia who is the type specimen of the Ancient North Eurasians, a population that also contributed to Native Americans.1

The second stream came with farming. Between 8,000 and 7,000 years ago closely related groups of early farmers appeared in Germany, Hungary and Spain, different from the local hunter-gatherers. They seem to descend from a common stock that spread along the Mediterranean to Spain and along the Danube to Hungary and Germany, and among people today they cluster with Sardinians. By 6,000 to 5,000 years ago, farmers across much of Europe had more hunter-gatherer ancestry than their predecessors: the two populations had been mixing.

The third stream came from the east. Haak's team, working with 69 ancient Europeans, showed that the Yamnaya steppe herders of Russia descended not only from eastern hunter-gatherers but also from a population of Near Eastern ancestry. Around 4,500 years ago the Late Neolithic Corded Ware people of Germany traced 75 per cent of their ancestry to the Yamnaya, documenting a massive migration into the heartland of Europe from its eastern periphery.2 This steppe ancestry persisted in all sampled central Europeans until at least 3,000 years ago and is ubiquitous in present-day Europeans.3 Fathers moved too. All seven Yamnaya males belonged to the M269 branch of Y-chromosome haplogroup R1b,4 and R1a and R1b, today the most common haplogroups in many European populations, seem to have spread into Europe from the east after 3000 BCE.

concepts.title: Pots, People and the Iberian Y Chromosome
concepts.contentHtml:
Did steppe ancestry move as a single wave? The Bell Beaker phenomenon offered a test. Its grave goods, stylised bell-shaped pots, copper daggers, arrowheads, stone wristguards and V-perforated buttons, spread across western and central Europe from around 2750 BCE, and archaeologists had long debated whether people moved or only ideas. In 2018 Iñigo Olalde and colleagues published genome-wide data from 400 ancient Europeans, 226 of them associated with Beakers. The answer was both.

Beaker-associated people in Iberia and central Europe showed limited genetic affinity, so migration was not a significant mechanism of spread between those two regions:1 there, the style travelled without the people. In Britain the opposite happened. The spread of the Beaker complex introduced high levels of steppe-related ancestry and was associated with the replacement of about 90 per cent of Britain's gene pool within a few hundred years.2 Britain's Neolithic farmers contributed only about a tenth of the ancestry of the people who came after them, and the Beaker newcomers continued an east-to-west expansion that had brought steppe-related ancestry into central and northern Europe some 400 years earlier.

Iberia adds a twist. In 2019 Olalde and colleagues assembled data from 271 ancient Iberians and found that by about 2000 BCE people with steppe ancestry had replaced 40 per cent of Iberia's ancestry but nearly 100 per cent of its Y chromosomes.3 Y chromosomes pass only from father to son, so a gap that large means the incoming lineages were overwhelmingly male, or that men with steppe ancestry had far more surviving children than local men, or both. DNA alone cannot tell you whether violence, marriage alliances or status lay behind it. It shows the pattern, not the story, and the story is where historians and archaeologists come back in.

concepts.title: Genes, Pots and Languages
concepts.contentHtml:
Haak's 2015 paper bore the title "Massive migration from the steppe was a source for Indo-European languages in Europe". Its data supported a steppe origin for at least some of the Indo-European languages of Europe, but the link between a population and a language is always an inference, because genes do not speak. Iberia shows the gap: by the Iron Age, steppe ancestry had spread into non-Indo-European-speaking regions as well as Indo-European-speaking ones, and present-day Basques are best described as a typical Iron Age population.1

Archaeologists objected to how such results were told. In 2018 Martin Furholt argued that the new genetic data were often presented in ways that recall traditional culture-historical archaeology, rightly criticised from the 1970s to the 1990s: the idea that shared material culture marks one social group, and that such cultures are homogeneous, clearly bounded entities.2 In vivid narratives of massive migrations, he wrote, cultural groups are once again likened to human populations and treated as external drivers of social change. The worry has a history. Early archaeologists such as Kossinna, writing in 1910, attributed successive cultures to wholesale migrations of peoples,3 and in the Nazi period nationalists twisted archaeological research to legitimise land seizures in Eastern Europe.

The genetic picture keeps sharpening all the same. The Yamnaya complex appeared around 3300 BCE on the steppes north of the Black and Caspian Seas. In 2025 Iosif Lazaridis and colleagues, with ancient DNA from 435 individuals, traced its origins to a Caucasus-lower Volga population. These people contributed about four-fifths of the ancestry of the Yamnaya and, entering Anatolia probably from the east, at least a tenth of the ancestry of Bronze Age central Anatolians, among whom Hittite was spoken.4 The team proposed that the speakers of proto-Indo-Anatolian, ancestral to both Anatolian and Indo-European, last formed a unity among these people between 4400 and 4000 BCE.5 It is a strong hypothesis resting on a modest signal, since earlier Chalcolithic and Bronze Age Anatolians lack this ancestry and only traces of it reach central Anatolia.

title: Plague Genomes and the Black Death
description: Pathogen DNA from teeth, Bronze Age plague, the Black Death's source and the selection debate

concepts.title: A Pathogen Genome from a London Plague Pit
concepts.contentHtml:
Ancient DNA can recover the killers as well as the killed. Teeth are the place to look: pathogens circulating in the blood at death can leave their DNA in the dental pulp, a sealed chamber inside the tooth. The Black Death of 1347–1351, caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, claimed an estimated 30 to 50 per cent of Europe's population in only five years.1 Yet differences between the epidemiology of the medieval disease and that of modern plague had ignited controversy over whether Y. pestis was really the cause.

London's East Smithfield cemetery is ideal evidence. Historical records indicate that it was established in late 1348 or early 1349 specifically to bury Black Death victims.2 Kirsten Bos and colleagues had already screened 46 teeth and 53 bones from the site for a plague-specific plasmid, and the reads showed the C-to-T damage pattern of authentic ancient DNA. In 2011 they used array-based capture on DNA from the dental pulp of the best teeth to enrich it for the bacterial genome. The result was a Y. pestis genome at 30-fold average coverage from victims securely dated to 1348–1350.3

The genome answered the controversy and changed the questions. The medieval organism is ancestral to most living strains and sits very close to the ancestral node of all Y. pestis commonly associated with human infection. The Black Death's bacterium was not exotic or extinct; its descendants still circulate. Comparisons with modern genomes revealed no unique derived positions in the medieval strain, which suggests that the disease's apparent extra virulence may not have come from the bacterium's own genes. Bos and colleagues argued that factors other than microbial genetics, such as environment, vector dynamics and host susceptibility, belong at the forefront of the discussion.4

concepts.title: From the Bronze Age to the Tian Shan
concepts.contentHtml:
Plague is far older than its pandemics. In 2015 Simon Rasmussen and colleagues screened about 89 billion DNA reads from the teeth of 101 Bronze Age people, sequenced originally for population history, and found Y. pestis in seven of them, aged from 2,800 to 5,000 years. The hosts belonged to cultures including the Afanasievo of the Altai, the Corded Ware of Estonia, the Sintashta of Russia and the Únětice of Poland. Plague was endemic in Eurasia at least 3,000 years before any historical record of pandemics.1 Yet these strains lacked ymt, the gene that made transmission by fleas possible, which was acquired before 951 BCE.2 Bronze Age plague probably caused pneumonic and septicaemic disease, but not the bubonic form.

Where did the Black Death itself begin? Two cemeteries in the Chüy Valley near Lake Issyk-Kul, in modern Kyrgyzstan, hold a clue. Their tombstones show a disproportionately high number of burials in 1338 and 1339, some giving pestilence as the cause of death.3 One reads, in translation: "This is the tomb of the believer Sanmaq. [He] died of pestilence." In 2022 Maria Spyrou, Philip Slavin, Johannes Krause and colleagues reported ancient DNA from seven individuals from these cemeteries, Kara-Djigach and Burana, and found evidence of Y. pestis infection in three of them.

Two reconstructed genomes represent a single strain, and it sits at the most recent common ancestor of the star-like emergence of four major lineages, branches 1 to 4, associated with the start of the pandemic.4 The Kyrgyz strain is ancestral to all published fourteenth-century genomes from western Eurasia, and comparisons with living plague in the Tian Shan region, where marmots and their parasites are the main reservoirs, support a local emergence. Earlier estimates had placed this diversification anywhere from the tenth to the fourteenth century; the Kyrgyz genome dates it to the first half of the fourteenth, shortly before the Black Death reached Europe.

concepts.title: Did the Black Death Change Our Genes?
concepts.contentHtml:
A disease that kills a third or more of a population in a few years should be a powerful agent of natural selection, and ancient DNA can test that directly by comparing people who lived before and after it. In 2022 Jennifer Klunk and colleagues characterised genetic variation around immune-related genes in 206 ancient DNA extracts from London and Denmark, from before, during and after the Black Death.1 Immune loci were strongly enriched for highly differentiated sites compared with non-immune loci, which they read as positive selection, and they identified 201 highly differentiated variants in the London data.

Their strongest candidate was rs2549794, near the gene ERAP2. The favoured allele is associated with producing a full-length rather than truncated ERAP2 transcript, with differences in cytokine response to2 Y. pestis, and with a greater ability of macrophages to control the bacterium in laboratory infections. The team also reported that protective variants overlap with alleles that are today associated with increased susceptibility to autoimmune diseases: a past pandemic, perhaps, shaping present-day disease.

In 2025 Alison Barton, Iain Mathieson and colleagues, including David Reich and Pontus Skoglund, replied in Nature that the evidence was insufficient. The enrichment in immune genes disappeared under an appropriate randomisation test; after an error in estimating allele frequencies was corrected, none of the four reported loci passed the original filtering thresholds;3 and those thresholds did not adequately correct for multiple testing. When they randomly relabelled samples as pre- or post-Black Death, the reported enrichment persisted, which means it could not be a signal of the plague. They also found no significant change in the frequency of the ERAP2 variant, in Klunk's data or in published data spanning 2,000 years.4

Klunk's team published a reply, and the question remains open. The laboratory evidence that ERAP2 variants affect the response to plague is one claim; whether the Black Death changed their frequency is another, and it needs larger samples than about two hundred people.

title: Sediments, the Ancient One and the Ethics of Sampling
description: DNA from cave dirt and Arctic clay, the Kennewick dispute, and who decides about ancestors

concepts.title: DNA from Dirt
concepts.contentHtml:
Hominin bones are rare, but caves are full of sediment, and sediment holds DNA. In 2017 Viviane Slon and colleagues used targeted enrichment of mitochondrial DNA to show that cave sediments are a rich source of ancient mammalian DNA that often includes traces of hominin DNA, even at sites and in layers where no hominin remains have been found. Screening many samples with automated help, they detected Neanderthal DNA in eight archaeological layers from four caves in Eurasia, and Denisovan DNA in a Middle Pleistocene layer near the bottom of the sequence in Denisova Cave.1

Sediment can be sampled systematically, layer by layer, in a way that bones cannot. Zavala and colleagues analysed 728 sediment samples collected in a grid from the Pleistocene layers of Denisova Cave, retrieving faunal mtDNA from 685 of them and hominin mtDNA from 175.2 The earliest hominin mtDNA was Denisovan, associated with early Middle Palaeolithic stone tools deposited about 250,000 to 170,000 years ago; Neanderthal mtDNA first appeared towards the end of that period, and modern human mtDNA at least 45,000 years ago. In 2021 Benjamin Vernot and colleagues went further and extracted nuclear DNA from cave sediments. They detected a population replacement in northern Spain about 100,000 years ago, accompanied by a turnover of mtDNA.3

The record now reaches far beyond the human story. Kjær and colleagues recovered environmental DNA from the Kap København Formation in Peary Land, North Greenland, now a polar desert, dated to around two million years ago. It describes an open boreal forest of poplar, birch and thuja,4 with hares, mastodons, reindeer, rodents and geese: an ecosystem with no present-day analogue. Sediment DNA has real limits, because each sample mixes DNA from many individuals and species and hominin DNA comes only in traces. But it turns every excavated layer into a potential genetic archive, even where not a single bone survives.

concepts.title: The Ancient One
concepts.contentHtml:
In July 1996 two students on their way to watch hydroplane races found a human skull in the shallows of the Columbia River at Kennewick, Washington. The nearly complete skeleton was about 8,500 years old. To the Umatilla, Yakama, Colville, Wanapum and Nez Perce tribes of the Columbia Plateau he was an ancestor, the Ancient One, and they asked for his return for reburial under the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA). Passed in 1990, the law provides that Native American remains found on federal land belong to the tribe with the closest cultural affiliation.

Eight anthropologists and archaeologists sued for the right to study him instead. Early study of the skull's shape had suggested that Kennewick Man was neither Native American nor closely related to the claimant tribes,1 and later measurements placed him closer to circum-Pacific groups such as the Ainu and Polynesians. Those morphological arguments shaped judicial decisions that NAGPRA did not apply, and in 2004 the scientists won the case.

Genetics reversed the verdict. In 2015 a team of geneticists sequenced his genome to about onefold coverage and found that Kennewick Man is closer to modern Native Americans than to any other population worldwide.2 Members of the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation, one of the five claimant tribes, took part with individual and tribal consent, and the Colville appear to descend from a population closely related to his. His mitochondrial and Y-chromosome lineages are found almost exclusively among Native Americans today.

In 2016 Congress passed a bill transferring control of the remains to the State of Washington, which conveyed them to the tribes.3 On 18 February 2017 some 200 tribal members and staff reburied the Ancient One at an undisclosed location on the Columbia Plateau.4 "We always knew the Ancient One to be Indian," said Aaron Ashley, a board member of the Umatilla.5 It had taken cutting-edge science nearly 20 years to reach the conclusion the tribes held from the start.

concepts.title: Who Decides About Ancestors?
concepts.contentHtml:
Every ancient genome begins by destroying a little of someone's skeleton, often a piece of the inner ear. Who should agree to that? In November 2020 more than sixty archaeologists, anthropologists, curators and geneticists representing over twenty countries met in a virtual workshop1 and drafted five globally applicable guidelines, published in Nature in 2021:

  • follow all regulations where the research happens and where the remains came from;
  • prepare a detailed plan before beginning any study;
  • minimise damage to human remains;
  • make data available after publication so that findings can be critically re-examined;
  • engage with stakeholders from the beginning of a study, with respect and sensitivity to their perspectives.2

The authors argued that recommendations grounded in North American debates do not always generalise. Ancient DNA, they wrote, has refuted myths of the purity of any population and falsified racist and nationalistic narratives, but emphasising group identity can cause harm where arguments about who is Indigenous have fed xenophobic and nationalistic politics. In their opinion it is inappropriate for genetic data to be used as an arbiter of identity.3

Critics replied in 2023. Kowal, Weyrich and colleagues argued that the guidelines do not sufficiently consider the interests of community stakeholders.4 They objected to a false separation of scientific and community concerns, to the consistent privileging of researcher perspectives, and to an open-data commitment that ignores Indigenous Data Sovereignty, the movement asserting Indigenous peoples' rights to control data about their communities and resources. Their conclusion was blunt: if a research team does not have the capacity to meaningfully engage communities, questions must be asked about the value and benefit of its research.5

The Kennewick case shows what is at stake on both sides. DNA vindicated the tribes' claim, yet it also meant sampling an ancestor they wanted reburied, not studied. Open data lets other scientists check a result; community control protects people from having their ancestors used in ways they never agreed to. Neither principle settles the other.
